context.concept_name: Meaningful contract examples and operation metadata

coverage.learning_objective: Make operation documentation actionable: add realistic examples and operation metadata to one route.

required_facts.statement: Set model_config = ConfigDict(json_schema_extra={"examples": [...]}) on a model to provide schema examples, or use Field(examples=[...]) for field-level examples.
Supply Body(openapi_examples={...}) for named request-body examples in the operation documentation.
Use tags, summary and description on a path operation decorator to describe and group the operation without changing its runtime behavior.
Validate proposed examples with Model.model_validate(example) before including them so their content agrees with the executable model.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Public examples should clarify an order operation's executable contract, not describe incompatible accepted data.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Set model_config = ConfigDict(json_schema_extra={"examples": [...]}) on a model to provide schema examples, or use Field(examples=[...]) for field-level examples.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Supply Body(openapi_examples={...}) for named request-body examples in the operation documentation. Use tags, summary and description on a path operation decorator to describe and group the operation without changing its runtime behavior. Validate proposed examples with Model.model_validate(example) before including them so their content agrees with the executable model.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: A documentation example should survive the same model validation a compatible input requires. Pick a synthetic order sample, validate it, and only then include it in schema or named body metadata. If the model has a quantity bound, use a sample satisfying that bound instead of a plausible-looking but invalid quantity. Descriptions and summaries can explain the operation, but they do not loosen the executable constraint. This gives the learner a practical review question: does the example illustrate the declared contract, or does it imply a different one? Publishing a model-valid synthetic sample clarifies the contract without changing runtime behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content:
For a synthetic order sample, use quantity 2 with a model whose quantity must be greater than zero. This places the compatible payload in model-level schema examples and validates it before publishing the documentation:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

example = {"quantity": 2}

class OrderInput(BaseModel):
    quantity: int = Field(gt=0)
    model_config = ConfigDict(json_schema_extra={"examples": [example]})

OrderInput.model_validate(example)
```

The sample's quantity satisfies the declared bound; an incompatible sample would mislead about accepted input. For field-level schema examples, use Field(examples=[...]); for named request-body examples, use Body(openapi_examples={...}). Add tags, summary and description to group and explain the operation without assuming they change behavior. The validated synthetic sample illustrates the declared shape rather than a different contract.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Descriptions do not change runtime behavior. Published examples should validate against their model.

video_need.reason: A tool demonstration can show the configured boundary and the evidence used to verify it. Focus: Make operation documentation actionable: add realistic examples and operation metadata to one route.

practice_anchor.objective: Add a realistic synthetic quantity example and operation metadata to one existing order route. Validate the sample, add model-level or field-level schema examples, and configure a named request-body example plus tags, summary and description without changing the handler's behavior.
practice_anchor.success: The quantity-2 sample passes OrderInput.model_validate. Schema metadata and the named body example use that validated sample. The route's tags, summary and description accurately describe its existing behavior, and its handler and quantity constraint remain unchanged.

live_code.required_skill: Configure example and operation metadata that agrees with an executable request model.
allowed_syntax: Python imports, assignments, dictionaries and lists
Named example dictionaries with summary, description and value keys
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide OrderInput with only quantity: int = Field(gt=0), an example dictionary containing only quantity, and an existing POST /orders handler that returns its validated input without persistence. Leave example metadata and descriptive decorator arguments unfinished.
live_code.observable_success: Executing OrderInput.model_validate(example) accepts {"quantity": 2}. Source review shows the same sample in schema and named request-body examples, descriptive operation metadata, and no changes to the handler body or quantity bound.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the relationship visible between the positive quantity constraint, the validated quantity-2 sample, schema examples, named body examples, and descriptive route metadata.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Documentation metadata clarifies the executable contract rather than implying another one.
Stay within the current objective: Make operation documentation actionable. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Select schema-valid examples and metadata communicating one actual operation contract.

coverage.learning_objective: Replace dependencies for isolated tests: override and restore one provider in an endpoint test.

required_facts.statement: app.dependency_overrides maps an original provider callable to a replacement callable that FastAPI uses when resolving that dependency in a test.
Assign app.dependency_overrides[original] = replacement, send the test request and assert the replacement's observable behavior.
Restore overrides after the test, such as by resetting app.dependency_overrides to an empty dictionary when no previous overrides existed, to avoid substitutions leaking into other tests.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An endpoint test needs a controlled provider result. Substitute at the declared dependency boundary and exercise its use through HTTP.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: app.dependency_overrides maps an original provider callable to a replacement callable that FastAPI uses when resolving that dependency in a test.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Assign app.dependency_overrides[original] = replacement, send the test request and assert the replacement's observable behavior. Restore overrides after the test, such as by resetting app.dependency_overrides to an empty dictionary when no previous overrides existed, to avoid substitutions leaking into other tests.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Map the original provider callable to a replacement in app.dependency_overrides. Send the request and assert behavior making the replacement observable, such as its synthetic value in the projected result. The mapping uses callables, not provider names or returned values. Restore the earlier override state afterward; reset to an empty dictionary when no prior overrides existed. Trace setup, request, assertion and restoration. Another test should not silently receive this replacement. Limit the override to the controlled input rather than substituting away behavior the test claims to verify.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Overrides left active can alter later tests. Restore the prior state rather than assuming automatic isolation.

video_need.reason: Running controlled success and failure cases makes the observable application boundary and assertions concrete. Focus: Replace dependencies for isolated tests: override and restore one provider in an endpoint test.

media.group_title: Replace a provider at the dependency boundary

segments.label: Map an original provider to a test replacement
segments.summary: A simple endpoint uses Depends to obtain a string from a provider. Initially, running the endpoint test prints 'actual user'. A replacement provider returns 'mock user', and the application’s dependency_overrides dictionary maps the original provider callable to that replacement. Running the test again prints 'mock user', demonstrating that FastAPI resolves the dependency through the replacement. The printed value demonstrates substitution, but the example does not assert that value or restore the override afterward.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the original provider callable becomes the dictionary key and the replacement becomes its value. The clip’s user-named provider simply returns a string; treat it as a controlled input.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates provider replacement through printed output, but omits an assertion of the replacement’s behavior and override restoration. The text covers both steps so later tests retain their intended provider behavior.

practice_anchor.objective: Override one string-returning provider in an endpoint test, assert its synthetic value in the endpoint response, and restore the original override state.
practice_anchor.success: The test request returns the replacement provider’s value, an assertion verifies that value, and cleanup restores the initially empty override dictionary even if the assertion fails.

live_code.required_skill: Map provider callables in app.dependency_overrides, exercise the endpoint through TestClient, assert the response value, and reliably restore overrides.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a hello-world endpoint, an original provider returning 'actual user', and a TestClient test scaffold. The endpoint includes the injected string under the response key 'user'. Begin with no overrides and leave replacement setup, assertion, and cleanup unfinished.
live_code.observable_success: A replacement returning 'mock user' is registered using the original callable as the key. The request yields 'mock user' under 'user', the test asserts that value, and a finally block restores app.dependency_overrides to an empty dictionary.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the original-to-replacement callable mapping, request, response assertion, and guaranteed restoration visible together in one endpoint test.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: A test substitutes a dependency at its declared boundary.
Stay within the current objective: Replace dependencies for isolated tests. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Determine which provider runs under an override.

coverage.learning_objective: Extract request metadata: declare one endpoint's metadata inputs.

required_facts.statement: Declare a request header with Annotated[Type, Header()] so the value is read from headers rather than interpreted as a query parameter.
Header converts underscores in Python parameter names to hyphens by default, and header names are case-insensitive; use alias or convert_underscores=False to control the name mapping.
Declare Annotated[Type, Cookie()] to bind a cookie by name, using a default when its omission should be accepted.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A handler needs a header and a cookie. Explicit source markers keep these metadata inputs from becoming ordinary query parameters.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Declare a request header with Annotated[Type, Header()] so the value is read from headers rather than interpreted as a query parameter.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Header converts underscores in Python parameter names to hyphens by default, and header names are case-insensitive; use alias or convert_underscores=False to control the name mapping. Declare Annotated[Type, Cookie()] to bind a cookie by name, using a default when its omission should be accepted.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Declare the inputs using Header and Cookie in Annotated types. A header parameter user_agent maps to user-agent by default because underscores become hyphens, and header names are case-insensitive. Use alias or control underscore conversion when the contract requires another mapping. Give a cookie a default when omission is accepted. Trace actual request names to their declarations instead of inferring the source from a metadata-sounding name. Keep source naming and omission behavior separate so a correctly bound cookie also has the intended requiredness.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A metadata-looking name does not automatically bind a header. The declaration and default underscore conversion matter.

video_need.reason: Annotated code supports the Header and Cookie declarations and underscore-to-hyphen conversion; a demonstration can help, but the text largely suffices.

practice_anchor.objective: Declare one endpoint's metadata inputs: bind user_agent to a request header and a cookie input by name, accepting omission of the cookie.
practice_anchor.success: The endpoint uses Annotated with Header() for user_agent and Cookie() for the cookie input. user_agent maps to user-agent regardless of header-name case, and the cookie has a default of None.

live_code.required_skill: Declare typed header and cookie parameters with explicit request-source markers and an omission default.
allowed_syntax: from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, Cookie
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an existing FastAPI application and a GET endpoint skeleton with user_agent and cookie parameters awaiting explicit source declarations. Keep the handler body unchanged so the task concerns metadata binding only.
live_code.observable_success: The completed signature declares user_agent as Annotated[str, Header()] and cookie as Annotated[str | None, Cookie()] = None. A supplied user-agent header binds to user_agent, and an omitted cookie binds to None.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the endpoint signature visible with annotations connecting user_agent to the case-insensitive user-agent header, showing alias and underscore-conversion alternatives, and connecting the cookie parameter to its named cookie and omission default.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Metadata binds through named request sources.
Stay within the current objective: Extract request metadata. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Determine header and cookie binding sources.

coverage.learning_objective: Interpret input validation errors: assert one invalid-input response.

required_facts.statement: FastAPI raises RequestValidationError for invalid request data and handles it before normal operation logic receives that input.
Assert the default invalid-input response status of 422 and inspect the JSON detail entries to identify the failed input location and error type.
Invalid request input is distinct from a model-validation failure in response or application code, which indicates a server-side bug rather than a client's invalid request.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Malformed order input should be rejected before normal handler logic. That differs from a validation bug in service-generated output.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: FastAPI raises RequestValidationError for invalid request data and handles it before normal operation logic receives that input.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Assert the default invalid-input response status of 422 and inspect the JSON detail entries to identify the failed input location and error type. Invalid request input is distinct from a model-validation failure in response or application code, which indicates a server-side bug rather than a client's invalid request.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Send a value that cannot satisfy a request field. Assert default status 422 and inspect JSON detail entries for failed input location and error type. Invalid input does not reach normal operation logic. Compare a validation failure while the service builds its own result: that indicates a server-side bug rather than this client-input rejection.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Not every model-validation failure is a client 422. RequestValidationError concerns invalid request data.

video_need.reason: Running controlled success and failure cases makes the observable application boundary and assertions concrete. Focus: Interpret input validation errors: assert one invalid-input response.

practice_anchor.objective: Assert one invalid-input response from the supplied order endpoint, including its default status and the rejected input's location and error type.
practice_anchor.success: The test sends the supplied invalid order input, asserts status 422, and verifies the expected location and error type in a JSON detail entry.

live_code.required_skill: Use TestClient to submit invalid request data and assert the default validation response.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a minimal order endpoint with a typed request field, an initialized TestClient, and one invalid order payload using only the endpoint's existing fields. Supply the expected error location and error type for that input. Leave the request and response assertions unfinished.
live_code.observable_success: The completed test passes by asserting response.status_code == 422 and matching a detail entry's loc and type to the supplied expectations, without changing the endpoint or its default error handling.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the invalid order request, the status-422 assertion, and the JSON detail entry's loc and type visible together so the rejected input can be traced to its response.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Invalid inputs are rejected before handler logic.
Stay within the current objective: Interpret input validation errors. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Locate rejected input and outcome.

context.concept_name: Configure established request-metrics instrumentation and verify counts, errors and latency with successful, failing and delayed requests

coverage.learning_objective: Configure and verify request metrics instrumentation: instrument one API with a maintained library and exercise three controlled requests.

required_facts.statement: Maintained request instrumentation records request and response counters and a duration histogram around the application boundary rather than requiring each handler to implement its own metrics.

Install the documented PrometheusMiddleware with app.add_middleware(PrometheusMiddleware, filter_unhandled_paths=True) and expose its metrics view with app.add_route("/metrics/", metrics), importing both from starlette_prometheus.
Use bounded nonsensitive labels such as method, matched route template and response status; filter unmatched paths so arbitrary requested paths do not generate unlimited metric series.

Verify wiring with controlled successful, expected-error and delayed responses, comparing request and response counter changes and the completed responses' duration observations with those known requests.

Interpret the selected middleware's measurement boundary accurately: its response counter is updated even for a raised exception, but its processing-time histogram is observed only when the inner application returns a response.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A metrics endpoint existing does not prove counters and durations measure intended request events. Compare maintained instrumentation against known requests.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Maintained request instrumentation records request and response counters and a duration histogram around the application boundary rather than requiring each handler to implement its own metrics.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Install the documented PrometheusMiddleware with app.add_middleware(PrometheusMiddleware, filter_unhandled_paths=True) and expose its metrics view with app.add_route("/metrics/", metrics), importing both from starlette_prometheus. Use bounded nonsensitive labels such as method, matched route template and response status; filter unmatched paths so arbitrary requested paths do not generate unlimited metric series. Verify wiring with controlled successful, expected-error and delayed responses, comparing request and response counter changes and the completed responses' duration observations with those known requests. Interpret the selected middleware's measurement boundary accurately: its response counter is updated even for a raised exception, but its processing-time histogram is observed only when the inner application returns a response.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Install PrometheusMiddleware with filter_unhandled_paths=True and expose the /metrics/ view from starlette_prometheus. Use bounded nonsensitive labels such as method, route template and status. Send a success, expected-error response and delayed response; compare counter changes and duration observations with those controlled requests. This middleware updates its response counter even for a raised exception, but observes processing time only when the inner application returns a response. Counts and completed-response durations therefore need not cover identical paths. Trace them before interpreting aggregates, and filter unmatched arbitrary paths rather than giving every requested path its own series.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A raised exception updates this middleware's response counter but does not produce its normal processing-time observation.

video_need.reason: A tool demonstration can show the configured boundary and the evidence used to verify it. Focus: Configure and verify request metrics instrumentation: instrument one API with a maintained library and exercise three controlled requests.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure one FastAPI API with the documented starlette_prometheus middleware and metrics view. Exercise one successful request, one expected-error request and one deliberately delayed request, then compare their metric changes against those known events.
practice_anchor.success: The API exposes /metrics/, filters unmatched paths and uses bounded nonsensitive labels. Each controlled request increments the relevant request and response counters once. Each response returned through the instrumentation boundary adds one duration observation, and the delayed response's duration reflects its controlled delay. Comparisons isolate the exercised routes from metrics-view traffic.

live_code.required_skill: Configure maintained request instrumentation and verify its counters and completed-response duration observations using controlled requests.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide one FastAPI app with existing successful, expected-error and delayed-response operations, plus a request harness that captures metrics before and after each controlled request. Leave middleware registration and /metrics/ exposure for the learner. Use only method, matched route template and response status to identify the exercised metric series.
live_code.observable_success: The configured middleware records the three known requests without per-handler metric updates. Before-and-after comparisons show the appropriate counter increments and completed-response histogram count increments; the delayed request produces a correspondingly larger duration contribution. The learner distinguishes a handled expected error that returns a response from an exception escaping the inner application: the latter still updates the response counter but does not add the normal processing-time observation.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make before-and-after request counters, response counters and histogram count and sum values visible for each controlled request, alongside its method, matched route template, response status and configured delay. Keep metrics-view traffic separate and distinguish returned responses from escaping exceptions.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Metrics correctness is checked against known events before production aggregates are trusted.
Stay within the current objective: Configure and verify request metrics instrumentation. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Verify successful, failing and delayed requests update counters and latency observations correctly with nonsensitive low-cardinality labels.

coverage.learning_objective: Preserve partial-update intent: implement one patch extraction.

required_facts.statement: Pydantic tracks explicitly supplied fields in model_fields_set; model_dump(exclude_unset=True) excludes fields that were not supplied.
Extract a partial update with update = model.model_dump(exclude_unset=True) so defaults for omitted fields do not overwrite stored values.
Explicitly supplied None remains supplied under exclude_unset=True; exclude_none=True separately removes None-valued fields and can erase an intentional null update.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A partial update must distinguish "leave unchanged" from "set to null." Presence carries intent separately from value.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Pydantic tracks explicitly supplied fields in model_fields_set; model_dump(exclude_unset=True) excludes fields that were not supplied.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Extract a partial update with update = model.model_dump(exclude_unset=True) so defaults for omitted fields do not overwrite stored values. Explicitly supplied None remains supplied under exclude_unset=True; exclude_none=True separately removes None-valued fields and can erase an intentional null update.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Compare the extracted update data itself before changing storage. An omitted note should be absent from exclude_unset output. An explicitly supplied None note should remain present. A supplied string should remain with its value. These cases encode three different intents under the update contract. A defaulted model value is not enough evidence to tell omission from explicit supply; model_fields_set and exclude_unset retain that distinction. If exclude_none is added, the null-valued case disappears for a different reason. Read the extraction options as intent rules rather than interchangeable cleanup flags. This is why a small output comparison is essential to explaining selective updates.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Stored order data has a note and quantity. An update supplying only quantity should not overwrite note with a default. Extract supplied fields with model_dump(exclude_unset=True); model_fields_set shows explicit fields. Now supply note as None. It remains in exclude_unset output because the caller supplied it and can represent an intentional null under the contract. Adding exclude_none=True removes it separately and can erase that intent. Compare omission, null and concrete values in extracted updates before applying them. The final value alone does not reveal whether a caller supplied the field.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: exclude_unset and exclude_none answer different questions. Removing None can erase an intentional null update.

video_need.reason: A small comparison table makes the contrasting cases clear; a moving demonstration would mostly repeat the text. Focus: Preserve partial-update intent: implement one patch extraction.

media.group_title: Preserve supplied-field intent in partial updates

segments.label: Extract supplied fields without including omitted defaults
segments.summary: A partial update should contain only fields the caller supplied. Calling post_data.model_dump(exclude_unset=True) extracts those fields from the request-body model. For example, when a caller supplies only a new title, an omitted content field must not enter the update through its default None value. Without exclude_unset=True, that default could overwrite existing content; with it, the extracted update contains only the supplied title.

bridge_note.before: Watch how exclude_unset=True keeps an omitted default out of the extracted update. The clip uses title and content; our worked example uses quantity and note.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains supplied-only extraction. The text additionally teaches model_fields_set and distinguishes explicit None from omission, including why exclude_none=True can erase an intentional null update.

practice_anchor.objective: Implement one partial-update extraction using update = model.model_dump(exclude_unset=True), then compare its results for an omitted note, an explicitly null note and a supplied string note.
practice_anchor.success: A quantity-only input produces only quantity in the extracted update. An explicitly supplied note=None produces a note key with value None, and a supplied string note retains that string. Omitted defaults never enter the extracted update.

live_code.required_skill: Extract explicitly supplied Pydantic model fields while preserving intentional null values.
allowed_syntax: Pydantic model construction with keyword arguments
string, integer, None and Boolean literals
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an OrderUpdate model with note and quantity defaulting to None, plus instances constructed as OrderUpdate(quantity=2), OrderUpdate(note=None) and OrderUpdate(note="Leave at reception"). Leave the supplied-field extraction assignment unfinished; no storage operations are needed.
live_code.observable_success: The extraction yields {"quantity": 2}, {"note": None} and {"note": "Leave at reception"} respectively. model_fields_set identifies quantity, note and note as the explicitly supplied fields in those cases.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make three order-update cases visible side by side: quantity supplied with note omitted, note explicitly supplied as None, and note supplied as a string. Show model_fields_set and the extracted dictionaries with exclude_unset=True, then contrast the null case when exclude_none=True is also added.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Presence carries intent separately from value.
Stay within the current objective: Preserve partial-update intent. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Distinguish absent, null and supplied fields.

coverage.learning_objective: Evaluate compatibility: review one schema change.

required_facts.statement: Changing an omittable request field into a required field rejects requests that were previously accepted, so a schema review must compare requiredness as well as types.
Tightening a type or field constraint can invalidate previously accepted client input; test representative previously valid inputs against the revised model.

Removing or changing a public response field or operation can change a client's documented expectations; compare the generated paths and response schemas with the previous contract before approving the change.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A revised order model can look cleaner while breaking previously valid clients. Review compatibility against accepted inputs and public outputs, not just new field names.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Changing an omittable request field into a required field rejects requests that were previously accepted, so a schema review must compare requiredness as well as types.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Tightening a type or field constraint can invalidate previously accepted client input; test representative previously valid inputs against the revised model. Removing or changing a public response field or operation can change a client's documented expectations; compare the generated paths and response schemas with the previous contract before approving the change.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Compare a previous omittable note field with a revised required one. An old request omitting note now fails. Likewise, a tighter quantity constraint may reject a previously valid quantity. Keep representative old inputs and validate them against the revision. On the output side, compare generated paths and response schemas before approving removed or changed fields or operations.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A matching type name alone does not prove compatibility. Requiredness, constraints, fields and operations also shape client expectations.

video_need.reason: A small comparison table makes the contrasting cases clear; a moving demonstration would mostly repeat the text. Focus: Evaluate compatibility: review one schema change.

practice_anchor.objective: Review one order request-schema change that makes note required instead of omittable. Validate representative previously accepted inputs against both models and identify the compatibility consequence.
practice_anchor.success: Demonstrate that a request omitting note passes the previous model but fails the revision, while a request supplying a string note passes both. Identify the new requiredness as client-breaking and preserve the previous default to retain omission support.

live_code.required_skill: Compare requiredness in Pydantic models and verify compatibility using previously valid request data.
allowed_syntax: dictionary literals with the note key or no keys
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide previous and revised order request models containing only note: the previous declaration is note: str | None = None, and the revision is note: str | None. Supply an empty request dictionary and a request dictionary containing a string note.
live_code.observable_success: Validation checks establish that both models accept the supplied string note, but only the previous model accepts omission. Restoring the default makes the omitted-note request valid again without changing its field type.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make previous and revised order contracts visible side by side: note requiredness, quantity constraints, generated paths, and public response fields. Pair each change with a previously valid input or documented client expectation that it could break.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Compatibility preserves previously valid expectations.
Stay within the current objective: Evaluate compatibility. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Identify client-breaking changes.

clusters.title: Bind and validate request metadata
clusters.reasoning: Header and cookie binding and request-validation errors fit the workflow of declaring metadata inputs and checking invalid request outcomes. All prerequisites for both are already available at tile start. Separate source/name binding from validation failure handling, and preserve the distinction between invalid client input and server-side validation bugs.

clusters.title: Preserve input intent as contracts evolve
clusters.reasoning: Partial-update extraction and compatible contract changes share the problem of preserving what a client request means. Both can be learned from prerequisites already completed before this tile. Keep omitted fields versus explicit null visible in the update sub-concept, and keep compatibility review as its own broader contract check rather than treating partial-update extraction as proof of compatibility.
